newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mideast conflict won't lie down at Cairo meeting.
newsitem.headline: Mideast conflict won't lie down at Cairo meeting.

text.p: Middle East conflict has reared its head at the Cairo economic conference despite overwhelming consensus on the formula for future prosperity -- free markets and integration into the world economy.

The one big agreement of the three-day Middle East and North Africa conference, which closes on Thursday, showed that a stalemate in Arab-Israeli peace talks can still scupper the type of regional projects favoured by the business community.

Egypt, Turkey and the U.S. oil company Amoco announced they would invest between $2 billion and $4 billion in a project to export Egyptian liquefied natural gas to Turkey by sea, instead of building a probably cheaper pipeline by land across Israel.
Israel again came under fire for preaching cooperation with its neighbours while strangling the Palestinian economy.

"The Israeli blockade (of the Palestinian territories) contradicts the principle of regional cooperation and the principles of this conference and previous conferences. There is a big consensus that such an attitude is unacceptable," Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said in an interview.

"The right message which emerged today at this conference is that the basis for cooperation in the region is Arab-Arab cooperation or cooperation between Arabs and other regions. The Arabs have become the focus," he told reporters from the Arab Israeli newspaper Kull al-Arab.

But otherwise the 1,500 business people at the conference, the third since Israel and the Palestinians started to make peace in 1993, have concentrated on pressing the internal economic reforms they say the region needs to catch up with the rest of the world after 40 years of intermittent warfare.

However, few of the Arab countries in Cairo have yet gone so far as to exclude the Jewish state from all of their plans. Most of their governments agree and have already embarked on classic programmes of privatisation, deregulation, trade liberalisation and monetary and fiscal reform along the lines of what has become the global orthodoxy.
"Everybody recognises the change here and everybody recognises the change will unleash huge potential," said Mohamed El-Erian of the International Monetary Fund's Middle East department.
The countries of the region have realised that they must put growth at the top of their agendas, become more outward looking and give the private sector a greater role, he added.
U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor tried to play down the effect of regional tensions on the conference, which was originally designed to help Israel integrate with its neighbours.
The focus of the conference has shifted because peace talks have stalled under the new rightwing government in Israel.
Egypt came close to postponing the meeting in protest at Israeli policy and for fear that few Arabs would turn up.
But Kantor said: "This conference has been a greater success than anyone predicted. Many Cassandras were saying this is going to be an enormous failure. It turned out to be the opposite."

"Business people, who are the most sensitive to political or other tensions, are voting with their feet and seeking joint ventures and investments in the region. You get a sense that we're moving in the right direction," he told reporters.
